claim: Perturbation of actin dynamics in the combined presence of latrunculin A, jasplakinolide, and Y-27632 significantly slowed down the endocytic retrieval of exogenously expressed Syph-pHluorin.
source: Perturbation of actin dynamics in the combined presence of latrunculin A, jasplakinolide, and Y-27632 significantly slowed down the endocytic retrieval of exogenously expressed Syph-pHluorin (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B, which demonstrate the effect of the drug cocktail on endocytic retrieval kinetics.

claim: This cocktail (latrunculin A, jasplakinolide, and Y-27632) was shown to preserve the existing cytoskeleton architecture while blocking actin assembly, disassembly, and rearrangement.
source: This cocktail was shown to preserve the existing cytoskeleton architecture while blocking actin assembly, disassembly, and rearrangement (Peng et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peng et al., 2011.

claim: Application of Y-27632 alone or a combination of latrunculin A and jasplakinolide had no effect on SV endocytosis kinetics.
source: Application of Y-27632 alone or a combination of latrunculin A and jasplakinolide had no effect on SV endocytosis kinetics, whereas combined use of Y-27632 together with jasplakinolide displayed a mild inhibitory effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Combined use of Y-27632 together with jasplakinolide displayed a mild inhibitory effect on SV endocytosis kinetics.
source: Application of Y-27632 alone or a combination of latrunculin A and jasplakinolide had no effect on SV endocytosis kinetics, whereas combined use of Y-27632 together with jasplakinolide displayed a mild inhibitory effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Impaired actin dynamics in the presence of latrunculin A, jasplakinolide, and Y-27632 did not impact the apparent level of SV exocytosis indicated by the maximal amplitude of Syph-pHluorin fluorescence.
source: Impaired actin dynamics in the presence of latrunculin A, jasplakinolide, and Y-27632 did not impact the apparent level of SV exocytosis indicated by the maximal amplitude of Syph-pHluorin fluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Perturbation of actin dynamics significantly delayed the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT in response to train stimulation with 200 APs at physiological temperature.
source: Perturbation of actin dynamics significantly delayed the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT in response to train stimulation with 200 APs at physiological temperature (Figure 1C and D), consistent with the results from exogenously expressed Syph-pHluorin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: vGAT exocytosis proceeded unperturbed under perturbation of actin dynamics.
source: vGAT exocytosis proceeded unperturbed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A dynamic actin cytoskeleton facilitates presynaptic endocytosis in hippocampal neurons.
source: Hence, a dynamic actin cytoskeleton facilitates presynaptic endocytosis in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that perturbation of actin dynamics delays endocytosis.

claim: shRNA-mediated depletion of Diaph1, encoding mDia1 (shmDia1), from hippocampal neurons led to significantly delayed Syph-pHluorin endocytosis and re-acidification in response to stimulation with 200 APs.
source: We confirmed that shRNA-mediated depletion of Diaph1, encoding mDia1 (shmDia1), from hippocampal neurons led to significantly delayed Syph-pHluorin endocytosis and re-acidification in response to stimulation with 200 APs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Re-expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type mDia1 fully restored normal endocytosis kinetics in mDia1-depleted neurons.
source: Re-expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type mDia1 fully restored normal endocytosis kinetics (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Impaired SV endocytosis in lentivirus-mediated mDia1-depleted neurons was observed if SV exo-/endocytosis was triggered by stimulation with 40 APs or 80 APs and probed with vGLUT1-pHluorin.
source: Impaired SV endocytosis in lentivirus-mediated mDia1-depleted neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) was also observed, if SV exo-/endocytosis was triggered by stimulation with 40 APs or 80 APs and probed with vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (vGLUT1)-pHluorin (Figure 1G and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Exocytic fusion of vGLUT1-pHluorin-containing SVs was unaffected by mDia1 depletion.
source: Exocytic fusion of vGLUT1-pHluorin-containing SVs was unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Co-depletion of the closely related mDia3 isoform tended to further aggravate the endocytic phenotype caused by mDia1 loss.
source: Co-depletion of the closely related mDia3 isoform tended to further aggravate this phenotype (Figure 1G and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and K) without impacting the apparent number of fused SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and L) or vGAT exocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: mDia1/3 depletion did not impact the apparent number of fused SVs.
source: Co-depletion of the closely related mDia3 isoform tended to further aggravate this phenotype (Figure 1G and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and K) without impacting the apparent number of fused SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and L) or vGAT exocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and L.

claim: mDia1/3 depletion significantly delayed the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT.
source: Furthermore, mDia1/3 depletion significantly delayed the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Application of IMM-01, a small molecule activator of mDia-related formins, led to a moderate but significant acceleration of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin.
source: Conversely, the application of IMM-01, a small molecule activator of mDia-related formins that acts by relieving autoinhibition (Lash et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1N), led to a moderate but significant acceleration of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 1K and L) but no change in apparent SV fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K and L, and by citation to Lash et al., 2013.

claim: IMM-01 acts by relieving autoinhibition of mDia-related formins.
source: Conversely, the application of IMM-01, a small molecule activator of mDia-related formins that acts by relieving autoinhibition (Lash et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1N), led to a moderate but significant acceleration of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 1K and L) but no change in apparent SV fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lash et al., 2013 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1N.

claim: IMM-01 application caused no change in apparent SV fusion.
source: Conversely, the application of IMM-01, a small molecule activator of mDia-related formins that acts by relieving autoinhibition (Lash et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1N), led to a moderate but significant acceleration of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 1K and L) but no change in apparent SV fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1O.

claim: Ultrastructural analysis of hippocampal synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons by electron microscopy revealed a reduction in SV density compared to controls.
source: Ultrastructural analysis of hippocampal synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons by electron microscopy revealed a reduction in SV density compared to controls (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The reduction in SV density in mDia1/3-depleted neurons was rescued upon prior silencing of endogenous neuronal network activity in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: This phenotype was rescued upon prior silencing of endogenous neuronal network activity in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: A similar, slightly more pronounced depletion of SVs was observed in hippocampal synapses from Diaph1 knockout (mDia1KO) mice.
source: A similar, slightly more pronounced depletion of SVs was observed in hippocampal synapses from Diaph1 knockout (mDia1KO) mice (Peng et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2003; Shinohara et al., 2012; Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E, and by citations to Peng et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2003; Shinohara et al., 2012.

claim: Mutant mDia1 lacking its N-terminal membrane-binding region (mDia1-ΔN) displayed reduced association with membranes in transfected HEK293T cells.
source: Mutant mDia1-ΔN displayed reduced association with membranes in transfected HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) and was unable to restore normal kinetics of Syph-pHluorin endocytosis in hippocampal neurons transfected with Diaph1-specific microRNA (shmDia1miR; Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Mutant mDia1-ΔN was unable to restore normal kinetics of Syph-pHluorin endocytosis in hippocampal neurons transfected with Diaph1-specific microRNA.
source: Mutant mDia1-ΔN displayed reduced association with membranes in transfected HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) and was unable to restore normal kinetics of Syph-pHluorin endocytosis in hippocampal neurons transfected with Diaph1-specific microRNA (shmDia1miR; Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: mDia may act on SV endocytosis by specifically promoting actin assembly at presynaptic membranes.
source: Hence, mDia may act on SV endocytosis by specifically promoting actin assembly at presynaptic membranes.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that membrane-binding is required for mDia1 function in endocytosis.

claim: Endogenous mDia1 is primarily localized to the presynaptic compartment, where it is concentrated at or very close to the plasma membrane.
source: This analysis revealed that endogenous mDia1 is primarily localized to the presynaptic compartment, where it is concentrated at or very close to the plasma membrane (Figure 3C and D), i.e., <50 nm away from the presynaptic membrane see Dani et al., 2010.
evidence: The claim is supported by multicolor time-gated STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and D, and by citation to Dani et al., 2010.

claim: Endogenous mDia1 is <50 nm away from the presynaptic membrane.
source: This analysis revealed that endogenous mDia1 is primarily localized to the presynaptic compartment, where it is concentrated at or very close to the plasma membrane (Figure 3C and D), i.e., <50 nm away from the presynaptic membrane see Dani et al., 2010.
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data and citation to Dani et al., 2010.

claim: Quantitative proteomic analyses of mDia1 immunoprecipitates from detergent-extracted mouse synaptosomes identified actin, Myosin IIB, and the small GTPase Rac1 as interaction partners.
source: Prompted by these results we dissected the interactome of mDia1 by unbiased quantitative proteomic analyses of immunoprecipiates from detergent-extracted mouse synaptosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). In addition to actin, we identified a variety of additional actin-regulatory proteins including Myosin IIB (Chandrasekar et al., 2013) and the small GTPase Rac1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, and by citation to Chandrasekar et al., 2013.

claim: The association of mDia1 with actin and Myosin IIB was confirmed by immunoprecipitation.
source: We confirmed the association of mDia1 with actin and Myosin IIB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and found Myosin IIB to be concentrated at or near the presynaptic plasma membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G) akin to the localization of mDia1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Myosin IIB is concentrated at or near the presynaptic plasma membrane akin to the localization of mDia1.
source: We confirmed the association of mDia1 with actin and Myosin IIB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and found Myosin IIB to be concentrated at or near the presynaptic plasma membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G) akin to the localization of mDia1.
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: The association of mDia1 with Myosin IIB is consistent with the inhibitory effects of the Myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin on SV endocytosis.
source: The association of mDia1 with Myosin IIB is consistent with the inhibitory effects of the Myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin on SV endocytosis (Chandrasekar et al., 2013; Soykan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chandrasekar et al., 2013 and Soykan et al., 2017.

claim: Several endocytic proteins previously implicated in SV recycling were enriched in mDia1 immunoprecipitates, including Synaptojanin1, Amphiphysin, Endophilin A1, PACSIN1/2, and Dynamin1.
source: Interestingly, we also observed an enrichment of several endocytic proteins previously implicated in SV recycling in mDia1 immunoprecipitates. These include the lipid phosphatase Synaptojanin1, the bin-amphiphysin-rvs (BAR) domain proteins Amphiphysin, Endophilin A1, and PACSIN1/2 and, the GTPase Dynamin1 (Chanaday et al., 2019; Gan and Watanabe, 2018; Saheki and De Camilli, 2012; Soykan et al., 2016; Figure 3E) as confirmed by immunoblotting (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3E and immunoblotting data in Figure 3F, and by citations to Chanaday et al., 2019; Gan and Watanabe, 2018; Saheki and De Camilli, 2012; Soykan et al., 2016.

claim: Application of the partially non-selective Dynamin inhibitor Dynasore led to a significant accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites marked by Bassoon.
source: Application of the partially non-selective Dynamin inhibitor Dynasore (Macia et al., 2006; Figure 3C and H) or expression of dominant-negative mutant Dynamin1 K44A (Figure 3G1) led to a significant accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites marked by Bassoon.
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and H, and by citation to Macia et al., 2006.

claim: Expression of dominant-negative mutant Dynamin1 K44A led to a significant accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites marked by Bassoon.
source: Application of the partially non-selective Dynamin inhibitor Dynasore (Macia et al., 2006; Figure 3C and H) or expression of dominant-negative mutant Dynamin1 K44A (Figure 3G1) led to a significant accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites marked by Bassoon.
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: mDia1 levels at the postsynapse were increased following Dynasore treatment or expression of dominant-negative Dynamin1.
source: mDia1 levels at the postsynapse were also increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Dynasore did not impact the levels or distribution of Bassoon or Homer1.
source: Dynasore did not impact the levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J) or distribution of Bassoon or Homer1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Endogenous presynaptic F-actin labeled by phalloidin was highly abundant at the postsynaptic compartment and also visible, albeit at reduced levels, in presynaptic boutons marked by Bassoon.
source: Multicolor gSTED imaging confirmed that F-actin labeled by phalloidin was highly abundant at the postsynaptic compartment. In addition, F-actin was also visible, albeit at reduced levels, in presynaptic boutons marked by Bassoon (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Inhibition of Dynamin in the presence of Dynasore significantly elevated presynaptic F-actin levels within the Bassoon area.
source: Inhibition of Dynamin in the presence of Dynasore (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or expression of Dynamin1 K44A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C) significantly elevated presynaptic F-actin levels within the Bassoon area.
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of Dynamin1 K44A significantly elevated presynaptic F-actin levels within the Bassoon area.
source: Inhibition of Dynamin in the presence of Dynasore (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or expression of Dynamin1 K44A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C) significantly elevated presynaptic F-actin levels within the Bassoon area.
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Actin polymerization-defective mutant mDia1 (K994A) failed to restore delayed vGLUT1-pHluorin endocytosis in mDia1-depleted hippocampal neurons.
source: We found that actin polymerization-defective mutant mDia1 (K994A) failed to restore delayed vGLUT1-pHluorin endocytosis in mDia1-depleted hippocampal neurons (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of mDia1/3 significantly reduced the amount of detectable F-actin within the Bassoon area.
source: We found that loss of mDia1/3 significantly reduced the amount of detectable F-actin within the Bassoon area (Figure 4A and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and E.

claim: Loss of mDia1/3 significantly reduced endogenous β-actin at presynapses in eGFP-Actb knock-in hippocampal neurons.
source: This assay confirmed the significant reduction in endogenous β-actin at presynapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4F and G using genome-engineered neurons.

claim: Treatment of mDia1/3-depleted neurons with jasplakinolide fully restored the kinetics of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin.
source: Treatment of mDia1/3-depleted neurons with jasplakinolide indeed fully restored the kinetics of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) and rescued presynaptic F-actin levels to that of controls (actin levels normalized to shCTR + DMSO, set to 100: shCTR + DMSO = 100 ± 6.3; shmDia1+3 + DMSO=47.7 ± 4.3; shCTR + Jasp = 150.6 ± 11.9; shmDia1+3 + Jasp=94.3 ± 11.5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Jasplakinolide treatment rescued presynaptic F-actin levels in mDia1/3-depleted neurons to that of controls.
source: Treatment of mDia1/3-depleted neurons with jasplakinolide indeed fully restored the kinetics of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) and rescued presynaptic F-actin levels to that of controls (actin levels normalized to shCTR + DMSO, set to 100: shCTR + DMSO = 100 ± 6.3; shmDia1+3 + DMSO=47.7 ± 4.3; shCTR + Jasp = 150.6 ± 11.9; shmDia1+3 + Jasp=94.3 ± 11.5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: mDia1/3 facilitates SV endocytosis by regulating presynaptic F-actin.
source: We conclude that mDia1/3 facilitates SV endocytosis by regulating presynaptic F-actin.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence showing the relationship between mDia1/3, F-actin, and endocytosis.

claim: Endogenous RhoA was mostly located within the presynaptic compartment.
source: Multicolor gSTED imaging revealed that endogenous RhoA was mostly located within the presynaptic compartment (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Interference with Rho function by co-expression of dominant-negative variants of RhoA and RhoB delayed SV endocytosis in response to stimulation with 200 APs without impacting the apparent levels of exocytosis.
source: Interference with Rho function by co-expression of dominant-negative (DN) variants of RhoA and RhoB (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or co-depletion of these Rho isoforms, by shRNA-mediated targeting of Rhoa and Rhob genes (shRhoA +B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), delayed SV endocytosis in response to stimulation with 200 APs without impacting the apparent levels of exocytosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B, and D.

claim: Co-depletion of RhoA and RhoB by shRNA-mediated targeting delayed SV endocytosis in response to stimulation with 200 APs without impacting the apparent levels of exocytosis.
source: Interference with Rho function by co-expression of dominant-negative (DN) variants of RhoA and RhoB (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or co-depletion of these Rho isoforms, by shRNA-mediated targeting of Rhoa and Rhob genes (shRhoA +B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), delayed SV endocytosis in response to stimulation with 200 APs without impacting the apparent levels of exocytosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, B, and D.

claim: RhoA activity was reduced in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1/3.
source: Consistently, we found that RhoA activity was reduced in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1/3 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RhoA-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Rac1 activity was significantly elevated in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1/3.
source: In agreement with the alleged antagonistic regulation of RhoA and Rac1 function (Lawson and Ridley, 2018), we found Rac1 activity to be significantly elevated in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1/3 (Figure 6B and C), e.g., under conditions of reduced Rho-GTP levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by Rac1-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 6B and C, and by citation to Lawson and Ridley, 2018.

claim: A similar increase in active Rac1 levels was observed upon pharmacological inhibition of RhoA/B in the presence of Rhosin.
source: A similar increase in active Rac1 levels was observed upon pharmacological inhibition of RhoA/B in the presence of Rhosin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Rac1-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rac1 was equally distributed between pre- and postsynaptic compartments in unperturbed hippocampal neurons.
source: Multicolor gSTED imaging showed that Rac1 was equally distributed between pre- and postsynaptic compartments in unperturbed hippocampal neurons (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Selective pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 reduced presynaptic actin levels.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that selective pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 reduced presynaptic actin levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C) and caused a delay in the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Selective pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 caused a delay in the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that selective pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 reduced presynaptic actin levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C) and caused a delay in the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: Rac1 inhibition appeared to further aggravate impaired vGAT endocytosis in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, although the effect remained below statistical significance.
source: Moreover, Rac1 inhibition appeared to further aggravate impaired vGAT endocytosis in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, although the effect remained below statistical significance.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations that did not reach statistical significance.

claim: Expression of constitutively active GTP-locked Rac1 (Rac1-CA) restored normal Syph-pHluorin endocytosis kinetics in mDia1/3-depleted neurons.
source: Expression of constitutively active GTP-locked Rac1 (Rac1-CA) restored normal Syph-pHluorin endocytosis kinetics in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, whereas Syph-pHluorin endocytosis was delayed upon expression of dominant-negative Rac1 (Rac1-DN) and exacerbated the endocytic phenotype of mDia1/3 loss (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Syph-pHluorin endocytosis was delayed upon expression of dominant-negative Rac1 (Rac1-DN) and exacerbated the endocytic phenotype of mDia1/3 loss.
source: Expression of constitutively active GTP-locked Rac1 (Rac1-CA) restored normal Syph-pHluorin endocytosis kinetics in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, whereas Syph-pHluorin endocytosis was delayed upon expression of dominant-negative Rac1 (Rac1-DN) and exacerbated the endocytic phenotype of mDia1/3 loss (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: No overt effect of Rac1 inhibition or overexpression of either Rac1 form on SV exocytosis was observed.
source: No overt effect of Rac1 inhibition or overexpression of either Rac1 form on SV exocytosis was observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F.

claim: Perturbation of Cdc42 did not significantly affect the kinetics of SV endocytosis in control or mDia1/3-depleted neurons.
source: Perturbation of the related Cdc42 protein, another actin regulatory GTPase Lawson and Ridley, 2018 found at synapses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–I), did not significantly affect the kinetics of SV endocytosis in control or mDia1/3-depleted neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J and K, and by citation to Lawson and Ridley, 2018.

claim: Synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons displayed an accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations that were found both in the vicinity of the active zone as well as distal from the synaptic contact area.
source: Synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons displayed an accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations that were found both in the vicinity of the active zone as well as distal from the synaptic contact area (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons displayed elevated numbers of endosome-like vacuoles (ELVs).
source: Moreover, we observed elevated numbers of endosome-like vacuoles (ELVs) (Figure 7A and C) that might serve as a donor membrane for SV reformation (Kononenko and Haucke, 2015; Kononenko et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2014) as suggested by the observed reduction in SV numbers in mDia-depleted neurons (compare Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and C, and by citations to Kononenko and Haucke, 2015; Kononenko et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2014.

claim: A prominent accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations was found in hippocampal neurons from mDia1 KO mice.
source: A prominent accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and endosome-like vacuoles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) was similarly found in hippocampal neurons from mDia1 KO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A prominent accumulation of endosome-like vacuoles was found in hippocampal neurons from mDia1 KO mice.
source: A prominent accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and endosome-like vacuoles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) was similarly found in hippocampal neurons from mDia1 KO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibition of Rac1 function by EHT 1864 led to the accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations.
source: Inhibition of Rac1 function by EHT 1864 also led to the accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 7A and D), whereas the number of endosome-like vacuoles was not significantly altered (Figure 7A and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and D.

claim: Inhibition of Rac1 function by EHT 1864 did not significantly alter the number of endosome-like vacuoles.
source: Inhibition of Rac1 function by EHT 1864 also led to the accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 7A and D), whereas the number of endosome-like vacuoles was not significantly altered (Figure 7A and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and E.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of Rac1 activity in neurons depleted of mDia1/3 further increased the number of plasma membrane invaginations significantly.
source: Pharmacological blockade of Rac1 activity in neurons depleted of mDia1/3 further increased the number of plasma membrane invaginations significantly, while the additional effect on the number of endosome-like vacuoles remained insignificant (Figure 7F, G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7F, G and H.

claim: The additional effect of Rac1 blockade on the number of endosome-like vacuoles in mDia1/3-depleted neurons remained insignificant.
source: Pharmacological blockade of Rac1 activity in neurons depleted of mDia1/3 further increased the number of plasma membrane invaginations significantly, while the additional effect on the number of endosome-like vacuoles remained insignificant (Figure 7F, G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7F, G and H.

claim: mDia1/3 loss and Rac1 perturbation exhibited similar phenotypes with respect to the length and width of tubular membrane invaginations.
source: mDia1/3 loss and Rac1 perturbation exhibited similar phenotypes with respect to the length and width of tubular membrane invaginations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Interdependent mDia1/3-Rho and Rac1 signaling pathways cooperatively act to facilitate presynaptic endocytosis and SV recycling.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that mDia1/3-Rho and Rac1 signaling pathways cooperatively act to facilitate presynaptic endocytosis and SV recycling.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence showing the cooperative action of these pathways.

claim: Loss of mDia1 either alone or in conjunction with the closely related mDia3 isoform slows the kinetics of SV endocytosis of exogenous pHluorin-tagged SV proteins and of endogenous vGAT without perturbing exocytic SV fusion.
source: We found that loss of mDia1 either alone or in conjunction with the closely related mDia3 isoform slows the kinetics of SV endocytosis of exogenous pHluorin-tagged SV proteins and of endogenous vGAT without perturbing exocytic SV fusion.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from multiple experiments.

claim: The endocytic phenotypes caused by mDia1/3 loss are accompanied by the accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations and vacuolar structures as well as an activity-dependent reduction of the total SV pool.
source: These phenotypes are accompanied by the accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations and vacuolar structures as well as an activity-dependent reduction of the total SV pool (Figures 1, 2 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1, 2 and 7.

claim: Endogenous presynaptic F-actin is reduced in mDia1/3-depleted hippocampal synapses.
source: (i) Endogenous presynaptic F-actin is reduced in mDia1/3-depleted hippocampal synapses (Figure 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Actin polymerization-defective mDia1 fails to restore normal endocytosis kinetics in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1.
source: (ii) actin polymerization-defective mDia1 fails to restore normal endocytosis kinetics in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1 (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pharmacological stabilization of F-actin by jasplakinolide rescues endocytosis in mDia1/3-KD hippocampal neurons.
source: (iii) pharmacological stabilization of F-actin by jasplakinolide (Figure 4) or (iv) expression of constitutively-active Rac1 to drive compensatory actin polymerization (for example via other formins and/ or ARP2/3) (Figure 6) rescues endocytosis in mDia1/3-KD hippocampal neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Expression of constitutively-active Rac1 to drive compensatory actin polymerization rescues endocytosis in mDia1/3-KD hippocampal neurons.
source: (iii) pharmacological stabilization of F-actin by jasplakinolide (Figure 4) or (iv) expression of constitutively-active Rac1 to drive compensatory actin polymerization (for example via other formins and/ or ARP2/3) (Figure 6) rescues endocytosis in mDia1/3-KD hippocampal neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: mDia1 and F-actin accumulate at presynapses under conditions of impaired dynamin-dependent endocytosis.
source: Moreover, (v) we find mDia1 (Figure 3) and F-actin (Figure 4) to accumulate at presynapses under conditions of impaired dynamin-dependent endocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Presynaptic actin facilitates SV endocytosis downstream of mDia/RhoA and Rac1-based signaling pathways.
source: Together with the observation that inhibition of F-actin dynamics (Peng et al., 2011) in the combined presence of latrunculin A, jasplakinolide, and Y-27632 (Figure 1) slows the kinetics of SV endocytosis, our data support the hypothesis that presynaptic actin facilitates SV endocytosis downstream of mDia/ RhoA and Rac1-based signaling pathways.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence and citation to Peng et al., 2011.

claim: The endocytic phenotype described for loss of mDia1/3 is substantially milder than that elicited by complete loss of β− or γ-actin.
source: The endocytic phenotype described here for loss of mDia1/3, however, is substantially milder than that elicited by complete loss of β− or γ-actin, likely reflecting the fact that several partially redundant pathways cooperate to promote F-actin assembly at synapses (see below).
evidence: The claim is an inference comparing the severity of phenotypes between different genetic manipulations.

claim: Several partially redundant pathways cooperate to promote F-actin assembly at synapses.
source: The endocytic phenotype described here for loss of mDia1/3, however, is substantially milder than that elicited by complete loss of β− or γ-actin, likely reflecting the fact that several partially redundant pathways cooperate to promote F-actin assembly at synapses (see below).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the comparison of phenotypes and the observation of compensatory mechanisms.

claim: In contrast to Actb or Actg1 KO hippocampal neurons, strong exocytic depression in response to train stimulation was not observed in mDia-depleted neurons.
source: In contrast to Actb or Actg1 KO hippocampal neurons (Wu et al., 2016) we did not observe strong exocytic depression in response to train stimulation in mDia-depleted neurons (e.g. Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–M) although we cannot rule out mild differences in synaptic strength and/ or release probability as observed in Rac1 KO hippocampal neurons and at the calyx of Held (Keine et al., 2022; O'Neil et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–M and by citations to Wu et al., 2016; Keine et al., 2022; O'Neil et al., 2021.

claim: Genetic or lentiviral induced loss of mDia1 or mDia1/3 partially phenocopies acute perturbation of formin-mediated actin assembly with respect to the accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations.
source: At the ultrastructural level, we find that genetic (KO) or lentiviral induced (KD) loss of the genes Diaph1 or Diaph1/2, encoding mDia1 or mDia1/3, respectively, partially phenocopies acute perturbation of formin-mediated actin assembly (Soykan et al., 2017) with respect to the accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous work cited as Soykan et al., 2017.

claim: Unlike acute formin inhibition, elevated numbers of post-fission endosome-like vacuoles were found in mDia-depleted hippocampal synapses.
source: Unlike acute formin inhibition (Soykan et al., 2017), we find elevated numbers of post-fission endosome-like vacuoles in mDia-depleted hippocampal synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous work cited as Soykan et al., 2017.

claim: The elevation of endosome-like vacuoles in mDia-depleted synapses correlates with a mild reduction of SV numbers, suggesting that mDia may have a further role in SV reformation downstream of the actual endocytosis reaction.
source: The latter correlates with a mild reduction of SV numbers, suggesting that mDia may have a further role in SV reformation downstream of the actual endocytosis reaction (Chanaday et al., 2019; Gan and Watanabe, 2018; Kononenko et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by experimental observations and citations to Chanaday et al., 2019; Gan and Watanabe, 2018; Kononenko et al., 2014.

claim: The identified function of mDia1/3-mediated presynaptic actin assembly in presynaptic endocytosis and SV recycling is consistent with the actin-binding properties of many endocytic proteins including Dynamin, PACSINs, or Epsins.
source: The identified function of mDia1/3-mediated presynaptic actin assembly in presynaptic endocytosis and SV recycling is consistent with the actin-binding properties of many endocytic proteins including Dynamin (Ferguson et al., 2009; Gu et al., 2014), PACSINs (Kessels and Qualmann, 2006), or Epsins, among others (McMahon and Boucrot, 2011; Merrifield et al., 2005; Saheki and De Camilli, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2009; Gu et al., 2014; Kessels and Qualmann, 2006; McMahon and Boucrot, 2011; Merrifield et al., 2005; Saheki and De Camilli, 2012.

claim: The comparably small size of the membrane invaginations that accumulate following pharmacological inhibition of formins or Rac1 or upon loss of mDia1 render an actomyosin-based constriction mechanism for SV endocytosis unlikely.
source: The comparably small size of the membrane invaginations that accumulate following pharmacological inhibition of formins (<100 nm) or Rac1 or upon loss of mDia1 (typically <150 nm, although larger ones are observed) render an actomyosin-based constriction mechanism for SV endocytosis unlikely (consistent with Sankaranarayanan et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on ultrastructural observations and citation to Sankaranarayanan et al., 2003.

claim: F-actin functions in presynaptic endocytosis via the formation of an F-actin ring that couples exocytic membrane compression to endocytic pit formation.
source: We rather favor a - possibly indirect - function of F-actin in presynaptic endocytosis via the formation of an F-actin ring that couples exocytic membrane compression to endocytic pit formation (Ogunmowo et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by citation to Ogunmowo et al., 2023.

claim: The abundance of large plasma membrane invaginations distal from the active zone at synapses following mDia1/3 and Rac1 loss of function supports a model where F-actin couples exocytic membrane compression to endocytic pit formation.
source: Such a model is supported by the abundance of large plasma membrane invaginations distal from the active zone where SV fusion occurs at synapses following mDia1/3 and Rac1 loss of function (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by ultrastructural data shown in Figure 7.

claim: mDia1 controls presynaptic membrane contractility.
source: Consistent with this, it has been shown that mDia1 controls presynaptic membrane contractility (Deguchi et al., 2016), e.g., via the recently identified presynaptic actin corrals visualized in genome-engineered rat hippocampal neurons (Bingham et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deguchi et al., 2016 and Bingham et al., 2023.

claim: Presynaptic actin corrals have been recently identified and visualized in genome-engineered rat hippocampal neurons.
source: Consistent with this, it has been shown that mDia1 controls presynaptic membrane contractility (Deguchi et al., 2016), e.g., via the recently identified presynaptic actin corrals visualized in genome-engineered rat hippocampal neurons (Bingham et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bingham et al., 2023.

claim: Presynaptic endocytosis is regulated by interdependent, yet partially redundant signaling for F-actin assembly downstream of Rho and Rac1.
source: A key result from our study is the finding that presynaptic endocytosis is regulated by interdependent, yet partially redundant signaling for F-actin assembly downstream of Rho and Rac1, e.g., pathways known to control linear and branched F-actin networks (Lawson and Ridley, 2018; Müller et al., 2020) that were shown to co-exist within hippocampal presynaptic boutons (Bingham et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lawson and Ridley, 2018; Müller et al., 2020; Bingham et al., 2023.

claim: Rho and Rac1 pathways are known to control linear and branched F-actin networks.
source: A key result from our study is the finding that presynaptic endocytosis is regulated by interdependent, yet partially redundant signaling for F-actin assembly downstream of Rho and Rac1, e.g., pathways known to control linear and branched F-actin networks (Lawson and Ridley, 2018; Müller et al., 2020) that were shown to co-exist within hippocampal presynaptic boutons (Bingham et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lawson and Ridley, 2018 and Müller et al., 2020.

claim: Linear and branched F-actin networks co-exist within hippocampal presynaptic boutons.
source: A key result from our study is the finding that presynaptic endocytosis is regulated by interdependent, yet partially redundant signaling for F-actin assembly downstream of Rho and Rac1, e.g., pathways known to control linear and branched F-actin networks (Lawson and Ridley, 2018; Müller et al., 2020) that were shown to co-exist within hippocampal presynaptic boutons (Bingham et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bingham et al., 2023.

claim: Loss of mDia1/3 causes the hyperactivation of the actin-promoting GTPase Rac1.
source: We demonstrate that loss of mDia1/3 or inhibition of Rho causes the hyperactivation of the actin-promoting GTPase Rac1 and that dual loss of mDia1/3 loss and Rac1 function results in synergistic inhibitory effects with respect to presynaptic endocytosis and ultrastructural defects (Figures 5—7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5—7.

claim: Inhibition of Rho causes the hyperactivation of the actin-promoting GTPase Rac1.
source: We demonstrate that loss of mDia1/3 or inhibition of Rho causes the hyperactivation of the actin-promoting GTPase Rac1 and that dual loss of mDia1/3 loss and Rac1 function results in synergistic inhibitory effects with respect to presynaptic endocytosis and ultrastructural defects (Figures 5—7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5—7.

claim: Dual loss of mDia1/3 and Rac1 function results in synergistic inhibitory effects with respect to presynaptic endocytosis and ultrastructural defects.
source: We demonstrate that loss of mDia1/3 or inhibition of Rho causes the hyperactivation of the actin-promoting GTPase Rac1 and that dual loss of mDia1/3 loss and Rac1 function results in synergistic inhibitory effects with respect to presynaptic endocytosis and ultrastructural defects (Figures 5—7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5—7.

claim: The signaling network that regulates presynaptic actin assembly may have been evolutionarily selected for plasticity and resilience.
source: These findings suggest that the signaling network that regulates presynaptic actin assembly may have been evolutionarily selected for plasticity and resilience.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed redundancy and compensatory mechanisms.

claim: A resilient network for the control of actin dynamics at the presynapse may help to explain the partially contradicting results from drug-based manipulations of actin and actin regulatory factors in different models of presynaptic neurotransmission reported in the past.
source: A resilient network for the control of actin dynamics at the presynapse may also help to explain the partially contradicting results from drug-based manipulations of actin and actin regulatory factors in different models of presynaptic neurotransmission reported in the past (Bleckert et al., 2012; Del Signore et al., 2021; Hori et al., 2022; Piriya Ananda Babu et al., 2020; Richards et al., 2004; Sankaranarayanan et al., 2003; Shupliakov et al., 2002; Wu and Chan, 2022; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a speculation supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Different pools of actin might be differentially amenable to drug treatments as a consequence of the association of actin filaments with molecules such as tropomyosin that render them resistant to drugs.
source: Moreover, accumulating evidence indicates that different pools of actin might be differentially amenable to drug treatments (Bleckert et al., 2012), e.g., as a consequence of the association of actin filaments with molecules such as tropomyosin (Gormal et al., 2017) that render them resistant to drugs, and/ or variations in the fraction of F-actin vs. monomeric actin pools (Higashida et al., 2008), providing a possible explanation for previously discrepant results.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bleckert et al., 2012; Gormal et al., 2017; Higashida et al., 2008.

claim: Variations in the fraction of F-actin vs. monomeric actin pools provide a possible explanation for previously discrepant results regarding actin function in endocytosis.
source: Moreover, accumulating evidence indicates that different pools of actin might be differentially amenable to drug treatments (Bleckert et al., 2012), e.g., as a consequence of the association of actin filaments with molecules such as tropomyosin (Gormal et al., 2017) that render them resistant to drugs, and/ or variations in the fraction of F-actin vs. monomeric actin pools (Higashida et al., 2008), providing a possible explanation for previously discrepant results.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bleckert et al., 2012; Gormal et al., 2017; Higashida et al., 2008.

claim: Presynaptic actin assembly via mDia/Rho and Rac1 is predicted to facilitate all forms of presynaptic endocytosis that operate on timescales of milliseconds to seconds.
source: We predict that presynaptic actin assembly via mDia/Rho and Rac1 facilitates all forms of presynaptic endocytosis that operate on timescales of milliseconds to seconds (Chanaday and Kavalali, 2018; Clayton and Cousin, 2009; Watanabe and Boucrot, 2017) and at many types of synapses (e.g. small central synapses, ribbon synapses, the neuromuscular junction), but further studies will be needed to test this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is a prediction/speculation supported by citations to Chanaday and Kavalali, 2018; Clayton and Cousin, 2009; Watanabe and Boucrot, 2017.

claim: Fast endophilin-mediated endocytosis (FEME) has been shown to be differentially regulated by actin and Rho GTPase family members.
source: We note that fast endophilin-mediated endocytosis (FEME), a process with resemblance to endocytosis at synapses (Watanabe and Boucrot, 2017), has been shown to be differentially regulated by actin and Rho GTPase family members (Boucrot et al., 2015; Renard et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Watanabe and Boucrot, 2017; Boucrot et al., 2015; Renard et al., 2015.

claim: It is not currently understood if and how RhoA/B and Rac1 GTPase activation is nested into the SV cycle.
source: At present we do not understand if and how RhoA/B and Rac1 GTPase activation is nested into the SV cycle and whether these GTPases operate at the same or different nanoscale sites and on the same or different membranes.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a gap in current understanding.

claim: It is not currently understood whether RhoA/B and Rac1 GTPases operate at the same or different nanoscale sites and on the same or different membranes.
source: At present we do not understand if and how RhoA/B and Rac1 GTPase activation is nested into the SV cycle and whether these GTPases operate at the same or different nanoscale sites and on the same or different membranes.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a gap in current understanding.
